newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich weighs in on census race controversy.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich weighs in on census race controversy.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich Friday evoked golf champion Tiger Woods as he weighed in on the controversy about how to define racial categories in the next census, calling for a single "multiracial" grouping.

Gingrich's support for a "multiracial" checkoff option is at odds with a Clinton Administration task force proposal that the 2000 census should allow people of mixed heritage to check off more than one of the four traditional racial categories.

"We should at least stop forcing Americans into inaccurate categories aimed at building divisive subgroups and allow them the option of selecting the option 'multiracial,'" Gingrich said in written testimony to a House subcommittee.
"I believe (that) will be an important step toward transcending racial division and reflectng the melting pot which is America," he added.

He and just about every other witness at the hearing made repeated references to Tiger Woods, the American golfing sensation who has white, black, Thai, Chinese and native American ancestors. Woods calls himself a "Cablinasian," an acronym for Caucasian, black, Indian and Asian.

The census is used to draw congressional districts and can affect the balance of power in Congress for a generation. Racial and ethnic data gathered in the census are used for dozens of federal programmes, ranging from enforcing the Voting Rights Act to monitoring housing discrimination laws to collecting health statistics.
In addition to the quarrel over race, Democrats and Republicans are feuding over whether to use a technique called sampling along with the traditional headcount.
Democrats say sampling yields a more accurate count, particularly of minorities. Republicans say it is an unreliable method that violates the requirement of a person-by-person tally.
The traditional census form allows for four racial categories -- black, white, Asian or Pacific Islander, and American Indian or Alaska Native.
A separate question about ethnicity deals with Hispanics and non-Hispanics.

Millions of Americans do not fit neatly into just one category. It is difficult for people to check off the race of just one parent and difficult to know whether those narrow choices allow an accurate reflection of the population.

The debate is whether to create one umbrella "multiracial" category as Gingrich proposed, or to stick with the traditional four choices but allow people to check off more than one. Tiger Woods, for instance, could qualify for all four.
